sentences.text: Montanoceratops was a small, four-legged plant-eater reaching a maximum length of 2.5 meters and a mass of 170 kilograms.
As an early member of the horned dinosaur group, this animal retained claws on its feet and teeth in its upper jaw rather than the toothless beak seen in later relatives.
Its overall size was similar to that of Protoceratops, measuring approximately 3 meters in total length.
One specific fossil specimen shows evidence of a severe injury that caused the bones in its tail to fuse together permanently.
Early researchers once believed the animal possessed a horn on its nose, but later analysis revealed this was actually a misplaced cheek horn.
The initial fossils were collected in 1916 by Barnum Brown and Peter C. Kaisen from the St. Mary River Formation on the Blackfeet Indian Reservation in Montana.
In 1942, Barnum Brown and Erich Maren Schlaikjer originally assigned these remains to the species Leptoceratops cerorhynchus.
Further material was found in 1986 by David B. Weishampel in Glacier County, and a well-preserved braincase was described in 2001 by Peter Makovicky.
The tail bones featured tall spines that created a deep cross-section, a structure that was not visible while the animal was alive.
Scientists propose that this flexible, deep tail served as a visual signal for communication with other members of the same species.
Charles Mortram Sternberg established the genus Montanoceratops in 1951 after determining the type material was distinct from Leptoceratops.
Later studies identified it as an advanced basal neoceratopsian, placing it within the family Leptoceratopsidae, a grouping confirmed by a 2012 study by Ryan et al.
This dinosaur lived during the Late Cretaceous, specifically between 83.6 and 66 million years ago, in the Maastrichtian stage of the Campanian to Maastrichtian periods.
Its environment consisted of wet, warm temperate to subtropical floodplains and streams bounded by mountains to the west, before a rapid cooling event near the end of the Cretaceous.
